newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. election nerves drag Asian shares mildly lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. election nerves drag Asian shares mildly lower.

text.p: Asian stock markets closed generally lower on Tuesday and even gainers were mostly limited by slim volumes as investors marked time ahead of the U.S. presidential election.

Hong Kong and Seoul were the hardest hit but for different reasons. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell sharply just before the close, ending 56.70 points or 0.45 percent lower at 12,502.70. Brokers attributed the drop to pre-U.S. election jitters and profit-taking from both local and overseas institutions.
"The market's fall was a bit of a surprise after the strength in the morning and must be short-term traders locking in profits ahead of the election," a broker with a large European house said.
"The chief worry is that we will see another serious imbalance in the U.S. Congress, said Kieren Hung, sales director at G.K. Goh.

South Korea's composite index fell for the second straight session, losing a further 13.77 points, or 1.84 percent, to a three-year low of 733.65. Brokers said investors dumped shares on continued fears that a huge oversupply of new stocks this month would spell disaster for the rudderless market.
The uncertain atmosphere was further dampened by the government's continuing anti-corruption campaign, which could further destabilise prices, they added.
Brokers and analysts said the recent jitters were due more to a shift in sentiment, sparked by collapse of the 750 support line, than a sudden change in fundamentals.
"Everyone knew about the ... oversupply of shares. It's now a psychological issue. People are really afraid to hold shares," said Choi Tae-hwan, head of sales at KLB Securities.

Tokyo closed lower after languishing in negative territory for most of the day, with the Nikkei 225 falling 40.73 points or 0.20 percent to 20,592.33. Brokers said that besides the U.S. election, trading was hampered by the launch of a new Japanese government and the formation of its policies.

Thailand, Indonesia, Australia and the Philippines were the day's only winners. Bangkok's SET index closed up 6.04 points at 919.01 as some investors took the opportunity to snap up cheap shares. But brokers said volume of 3.05 billion baht indicated that the market was focusing on political developments ahead of the general election on November 17.
Jakarta's composite index rose 5.562 points or 0.96 percent to 583.87, Sydney's all ordinaries index added 4.1 points to 2,361.6, and Manila's composite index added 11.04 to 2,987.18.

All other markets were lower. Taiwan's weighted index ended 18.47 points or 0.28 percent lower at 6,604.14, running out of steam in the final hour after gaining nearly 300 points in the three previous sessions.

Singapore's Straits Times industrials index ended 5.55 points off at 2,070.23, Malaysia's composite index shed 0.26 to 1,176.81, Bombay's BSE Sensex was down 21.12 at a provisional 3,071.6, and New Zealand's top 40 eased 3.04 points to 2,311.46.
The dollar stalled against the yen and mark in Tokyo, activity inhibited by uncertainty over Russian President Boris Yeltsin's heart surgery and ahead of the U.S. election.
At 1150 GMT the greenback was quoted at 113.78/83 yen and 1.5119/24 marks.
SIMEX December Brent futures were slightly fimer in late trade, finding modest support from jitters over Yeltsin's health.
December Brent was last traded at US$22.30 per barrel, up two cents from London's Monday close.
Hong Kong gold ended higher than the New York close on overseas buying and dealers said any selling interest from Japan was absorbed by professional buying.
Bullion ended at US$379.00/50 an ounce against New York's $378.60/379.00 close on Monday.
